text: Revenge here requires an apprenticeship: to kill the men who killed his father, a nobleman must first get himself hired by them. Albert Parker's 1926 adventure spends most of its ninety-four minutes on the strain of that arrangement rather than on grief. Every gesture the hero makes among the crew is double, convincing to the pirates and calculated by him, and the largest set piece, a merchant ship taken single-handed, plays less as a fight than as an audition before men who would hang him for one wrong move. Then a passenger of royal blood is found aboard, and the disguise acquires a witness with no reason to protect it. Silent adventure wanted physical proof of character. This is a film about a body performing a lie in front of experts.

Captain Nemo's submarine is not an instrument of exploration here; it is a vehicle for a grudge with a name and an address. Stuart Paton's film sends the machine across twenty thousand leagues after Charles Denver, the man held responsible for the death of Princess Daaker, so the ocean stops being a frontier and becomes a distance to be closed. Nineteen sixteen set hard limits on what could be shown of the deep, and the ambition of the thing is measured by how much is attempted at all rather than reported in title cards. Ninety-nine minutes. Inside the adventure sits an old injury, a daughter carried off on a yacht, and a man who answered both by building an engine and going under. The future arrives here as an instrument of mourning, which is a strange thing for 1916 to have understood.

A romance that ties its leading man up and has him beaten is doing something other than swooning. Sixty-nine minutes long, George Fitzmaurice's 1926 film gives Ahmed an inherited name, a secret meeting place, and Yasmin, who dances at the front of her father's company of tricksters. What follows — capture, a ransom demand, injury he did not see coming — turns the affair into a question of what she knew and when. Desert pictures of the period ran on abduction and disguise, and this one is unusually direct about where its heat comes from: a man displayed, admired, and hurt. It moves fast because a film this short has no slack in it. The interesting part is the suspicion between two people who had to meet in secret before anyone laid a hand on them.

Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings moved to the Florida backwaters in the 1930s to be left alone, which turned out to be different from being alone. Martin Ritt's film gives her a little over two hours of interruption: men with intentions, editors sending opinions from a long way off, neighbours who cannot place her and see no reason to pretend otherwise. Filming a writer is hard because the work is invisible, and the solution here is to put the labour outside the house, in the grove and the water and the company of people who already know the ground she is trying to learn. The Yearling comes out of that ground. So the film has to watch her taking from the neighbours what she will later sell, and it does not entirely let her off. Ritt keeps the manners exact and the temperature low.

In 1938 an American studio released a love story about three German veterans, and the date sits in the room with them. Frank Borzage films the friendship first — the habits three survivors keep up because the alternative is being alone with what they came back from — and only afterwards the woman all three of them love. Her tuberculosis is stated plainly and early, so the film is never suspenseful about her health; it is suspenseful about whether devotion can be organised among four people without anyone being cheated. Borzage shoots affection as shelter, and the years after that war supply the weather. Ninety-eight minutes, made in Hollywood about a Germany that in 1938 was nobody's neutral subject. The tenderness is the method here, not the trim.

The whole engine of the film is a scheduling problem: three girls, one boy, and no way to be in two places at once. George B. Seitz made it in 1938, ninety-one minutes, and treats adolescent romance as logistics — promises given separately that cannot all be honoured on the same evening, each one reasonable when it was made. Comedy of this kind needs a town small enough that everybody's business overlaps and a hero whose panic is sincere. Andy is not scheming; he has agreed to too much and the calendar is closing in. What keeps it alive is timing and the faces doing it, because the plot holds no surprises and was never meant to. A boy talking himself into three futures at once, hoping none of them meet.

The soldier and the chorus girl exist to give the design somewhere to happen. Busby Berkeley's 1943 musical keeps its plot thin — a romance, then a posting to the Pacific — and hangs an hour and three quarters of colour on it. The Academy gave the film its award for colour art direction, which is an honest account of where the effort went: the argument is made in scale, arrangement, and hue rather than in dialogue. What is strange, and worth staying with, is the arithmetic of 1943. An audience is shown a man sent to the Pacific in the first reel and then handed spectacle in place of reassurance, and the film performs that exchange without flinching from either half. The romance is slight. The colour is not, and neither is the thing it is covering.

Two houses in a small Mississippi town in 1916, and the distance between the porches is most of the film. Peter Glenville takes just under two hours and almost no geography: a woman with rigid habits and a strong will, the young man next door with neither, and a code of manners that makes every honest sentence expensive. The period does real work. In that town, in that year, what she wants has no vocabulary available to it that is not religious or shameful, and the tension comes from watching her hunt for a third one. Made in 1961, the picture can go further than an earlier decade would have allowed and still cannot name the thing outright, so the acting carries what the writing withholds. Heat is a condition rather than a setting; the colour art direction took an Academy Award.

Gerald talks in sound effects, and the household has to decide whether that counts as a problem. Robert Cannon's eight-minute cartoon takes a premise that could only exist after sound came in — the boings land exactly where the words should be — and lets everything else follow from the family's reaction. Dr. Seuss wrote the story with Bill Scott, and the rhyme keeps the surface light over material that is plainly about a child nobody can understand and a house that would prefer him ordinary. It took that year's Academy Award for animated short. Eight minutes allows no consolation scene and no long explanation, so the film advances by cut and by noise, and the audience hears what the parents hear on the same terms they do.

The killing is an accident; the conversion is not, and the film spends its length on the distance between the two. King Vidor made it in 1929, when a picture built around singing was still an experiment in a new technology, and the music here is not ornament: work, sermon, and congregation are how the story moves. A laborer takes the pulpit and discovers that persuasion works on the persuader as well, which is the most interesting pressure in it. That a major American production of that year was built around Black performers and Black religious music cannot be separated from the way its camera looks at them, and both facts are in every scene. Vidor's direction was recognised by the Academy. A hundred minutes, and the weight rests on a man holding authority that arrived by accident.

Bail has to be posted in Santa Fe, and the two Northern Cheyenne men who mean to post it are starting from Montana. An errand makes good structure: fixed destination, running clock, a sister in a cell on a charge that somebody else arranged. The road keeps turning into something older than the errand, and the film lets that happen at its own pace, without treating either traveller as the one who has it right. Jonathan Wacks shot it in 1989 in a comic register, which is the choice that keeps the anger legible instead of sanded down; the jokes and the grievance come from the same place. It took the dramatic filmmaker's trophy at Sundance. Ninety-one minutes, most of it highway, and the cell at the far end stops the comedy from floating away.

Daisy Miller is not a mystery; the people around her have decided that she must be one. Peter Bogdanovich's 1974 film is about that decision and its manners — how a set of Americans abroad convert a young woman's directness into evidence, and how Frederick Winterbourne, who is placed to stop it, would rather keep observing her. The comedy sits in the gap between what a drawing room says and what it means. The cost falls on the one person not fluent in the code. Ninety-one minutes, period costume that the Academy singled out, and a tone that declines to warm up. Conversation is the main event, so the picture stands or falls on rhythm: the timing of an interruption, the length of a pause before an answer. It is a film about reputation, which is to say about other people talking.

Four thousand dollars is gone, and so is the man who was holding it. Wayne Wang's 1982 film sends two cabbies around San Francisco's Chinatown to ask after him, and the answers keep being about something else: who is counted as Chinese, who is counted as American, and what a name is worth on either side of a door. The missing-person structure is used for access rather than suspense — a vanished man is a reason to knock. The city arrives mostly from the front seat of a taxi, at the pace of a working shift. What accumulates is a portrait built from people who do not agree about the person they are describing, and the film is content to leave the disagreement unresolved. Seventy-six minutes, dry, unhurried, and deliberate about staying small.

Cheese, eaten late and in quantity, is the alibi for everything the camera does next. Seven minutes, 1906, taken from Winsor McCay's newspaper strip, and the arrangement is exact: the meal licenses the dream, and the dream licenses the tricks. Edwin S. Porter had the period's whole toolkit available — whatever a camera and a darkroom could be made to fake — and a premise that authorises all of it without owing anyone a story. The strip repeated that premise by design; the film borrows it whole and adds motion. The joke is a small appetite punished out of all proportion, with the sufferer at no point in charge of the punishment. One reel, no padding, and what a 1906 audience was handed was a man's digestion staged as a special effect.
